entities.name: Dietrich Schenk von Erbach
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dietrich Schenk von Erbach, who served as Archbishop and Elector of Mainz from 1434 until his death on May 15, 1459, was a pivotal figure in the complex political and ecclesiastical landscape of 15th-century Western Europe. His tenure coincided with the twilight of the Conciliar Movement, the ongoing fragmentation of the Holy Roman Empire, and the nascent stages of the printing revolution. As one of the most powerful Prince-Electors, Dietrich wielded significant influence, mediating disputes between imperial and papal factions while working to consolidate the temporal and spiritual authority of his archdiocese, a crucial territory within the German realm.

His archiepiscopate was marked by active participation in imperial affairs, including attendance at several Imperial Diets and a prominent role at the Council of Basel (1431–1449), where he initially supported its reformist agenda before aligning with Pope Eugenius IV in 1442, a strategic move to secure papal recognition and avoid further schism. Dietrich skillfully navigated the shifting allegiances of the electors and the Emperor Frederick III, contributing to the resolution of the Mainz Schism of 1449 and the subsequent Concordat of Vienna (1448), which helped define relations between the papacy and German princes. Crucially, his administration provided a stable environment in Mainz, which proved instrumental for the experiments of Johannes Gutenberg, who developed his revolutionary movable type printing press in the city during this period, possibly with indirect support or at least tolerance from the archiepiscopal court.
